title: Futures and promises
summary: The promise-future channel, exceptions and broken promises, std::async launch policies and their traps, packaged_task, and shared_future.

clips.title: A one-shot channel
clips.question: How does a value, or an exception, travel from a promise to its future?

scenes.say: Futures, question one. How does a value, or an exception, travel from a promise in one thread to a future in another? Pause and answer out loud.

props.question: How does a value travel from a promise to its future?

scenes.say: A promise and its future share one heap allocated state. The consumer calls get, and blocks until that state is ready. The producer calls set value. The state stores it, and wakes the consumer. Get moves the value out, so it can be called only once. If the work throws, set exception stores the exception instead, and get rethrows it in the consumer's thread. And if the promise is destroyed without setting anything, get throws a broken promise error, instead of waiting forever.

steps.note: promise + future share one heap-allocated state
get() blocks until the state is ready
State is ready: the consumer wakes
get() moves the value out: call it once
get() rethrows in the consumer's thread

clips.title: std::async traps
clips.question: What do async's launch policies do, and how can async silently run synchronously?

scenes.say: Question two. What do the launch policies of standard async do? And how can a call to async silently run synchronously? Pause and answer out loud.

Launch async runs the function as if on a new thread, starting now. Launch deferred runs nothing until get, and then runs on the calling thread. With no policy, the library may choose either. Two traps. A future from async, with the async policy, blocks in its destructor until the task finishes. Ignore the return value, and the temporary dies right there, so the call waits: no background work at all. And a deferred task never becomes ready on its own, so a loop waiting for ready spins forever. Check for deferred first, or always pass a policy.

props.title: Two traps

highlights.note: ~future waits: a discarded result is a sync call
Detect deferred, or pass a policy

clips.title: packaged_task and shared_future
clips.question: When do you need packaged_task, and when shared_future?

scenes.say: Question three. Promise, packaged task, and async all produce futures. When do you need packaged task? And when a shared future? Pause and answer out loud.

Three ways to get a future. A promise is the raw channel: you decide when to set the value. Packaged task wraps a callable, and sets the value when it's called, wherever and whenever that is. Async wraps the callable and also decides where it runs.

items.label: std::packaged_task
items.title: A callable + its future
items.body: You decide where and when it runs.

items.label: std::async
items.title: Callable + a thread
items.body: The library runs it for you.

scenes.say: That makes packaged task the building block of thread pools. Submit wraps the function, keeps the future for the caller, and moves the task into a queue. It's move only: one task, one result. A worker thread pops it, and calls it, which stores the value, or the exception. A plain future has one reader. When several threads need the same result, call share: shared future is copyable, and every copy's get returns it.

props.title: The thread-pool pattern

highlights.note: Each copy's get() sees the result

scenes.say: To recap. A promise and future are a one shot channel, carrying a value, or an exception. Destroying an unset promise breaks it. The future from async waits in its destructor. And packaged task is how thread pools hand back results.

items.text: promise → future: one value or one exception.
async's future waits in its destructor.
